general_guides.title: Termite signs and next steps
paragraphs: Termite activity can be difficult to assess from a single sign. Mud-like shelter tubes, damaged wood, or discarded wings may be reasons to arrange a closer inspection; these signs do not confirm an infestation on their own.
Avoid disturbing suspected activity before an assessment. A pest professional can inspect the affected material and explain whether a termite service is appropriate for the property.

general_guides.title: Reducing cockroach attractants
paragraphs: Food residue, accessible water, and undisturbed gaps can make indoor spaces more inviting to cockroaches. Keeping food sealed, cleaning spills, and addressing leaks are practical steps that support a pest-management plan.
If activity continues, note where and when it is seen and request an assessment. The suitable treatment depends on the site and should be paired with clear preparation and aftercare instructions.

general_guides.title: Rodent prevention basics
paragraphs: Store food and waste in closed containers and check for openings around doors, service lines, and storage areas. These housekeeping and exclusion steps can reduce access to food and shelter but do not replace an inspection when rodent activity is present.
A professional can assess signs such as droppings or gnawing and discuss a suitable rodent-management plan for the property.

general_guides.title: Bed bug inspection guidance
paragraphs: When checking for possible bed bugs, inspect mattress seams, bed frames, and nearby furniture for insects or spotting. A single mark is not enough to identify the pest, so avoid moving potentially affected items between rooms.
If you suspect bed bugs, contact a pest professional for identification and treatment guidance. Follow the preparation and follow-up instructions provided for the selected service.

general_guides.title: Mosquito source reduction
paragraphs: Mosquito management includes checking for standing water where larvae may develop and keeping water containers covered or emptied where practical. Door and window screens can also help limit entry indoors.
Fogging may be one part of a broader vector-control approach, but it does not remove breeding sources. Ask the service team which measures suit the site and current concern.

general_guides.title: Wood borer signs
paragraphs: Small exit holes or fine powder around timber can have several causes and do not by themselves identify a wood-boring pest. Note the affected item and location, and avoid applying an unverified product to the wood.
An inspection can help identify the cause and determine whether wood borer control is suitable. Treatment recommendations depend on the material and extent of the issue.

general_guides.title: Planning commercial pest management
paragraphs: Commercial pest management works best when inspection, sanitation, monitoring, and any agreed treatment are considered together. Keeping records of sightings and corrective actions can help a business and its service provider review recurring concerns.
For scheduled support, discuss the premises, operating hours, and service requirements before agreeing an AMC/IPM scope and visit schedule.

general_guides.title: Fly management and sanitation
paragraphs: Covered waste, clean drains, and screened openings can support fly prevention in places where food is prepared or stored. These measures address common attractants and entry points but may not resolve an established pest problem by themselves.
A site assessment can help identify practical sanitation or exclusion steps and whether a fly-management system is suitable for the premises.

general_guides.title: Preparing for a pest inspection
paragraphs: Before an inspection, note where pest activity occurs, when it is noticed, and which rooms or materials are affected. Share this information with the service team and ask what access or preparation is needed.
Do not assume that every treatment uses the same method. Follow the instructions given for the specific service and property.

general_guides.title: Keeping a pest-management plan useful
paragraphs: A practical pest-management plan considers the pest identified, the property conditions, and the steps needed after service. Clear communication about access, occupants, and business operations helps the team discuss suitable timing and precautions.
For recurring commercial needs, review monitoring notes and agreed actions with the provider so any scheduled plan remains aligned with the premises.
